idiom_name: mixin module (include Comparable/Enumerable) or module_function servant
implementation_notes: Ruby's servant is a module: include Comparable grants every class that defines <=> the whole comparison protocol, include Enumerable grants the traversal protocol to every class that defines each, so the behaviour is written once and the serviced class supplies only the primitive - the capability interface is that single method, and the serviced classes inherit the behaviour without sharing any other ancestor. When the serviced objects should not gain the methods, the same module is used as a function servant via module_function or extend self and called as MoveServant.move_to(shape, pos) with the object as an argument; refinements are the modern way to scope such additions lexically instead of globally.
code_sketch:
module Movable                      # the servant: one module, many unrelated hosts
  def move_to(pos) = self.position = pos
  def move_by(dx, dy) = move_to(Position.new(position.x + dx, position.y + dy))
end

class Circle                        # owns only the primitive the module needs
  include Movable
  attr_accessor :position
end

# function form: module MoveServant; module_function; def move_to(shape, pos) ... end; end
pitfalls: include inserts the module into the ancestor chain for every instance: a name clash silently shadows (or is shadowed by) the class's own methods, and the serviced class now advertises behaviour it does not implement - keep module method names role-based and check Module#ancestors.

module_function copies the methods onto the module's singleton at definition time, so a later redefinition does not propagate to the copy, and included methods and module methods see self differently - do not mix the two styles in one module.
Because inclusion is opened to every class, adding the module to a core class (String, Array) patches the whole process; prefer refinements or an explicit servant object for third-party types.
sources: Ruby documentation, module Comparable - 'used by classes whose objects may be ordered', the class must define <=> and the mixin implements the comparison operators and between?; https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/Comparable.html
Ruby documentation, module Enumerable - include it and define each, and the mixin supplies the whole collection protocol; https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/Enumerable.html
Ruby documentation, class Module - include, prepend and module_function semantics; https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/Module.html
